performers: Royal Choral Society; Royal Albert Hall Orchestra; Malcolm Sargent, conductor
intro: Malcolm Sargent conducts the Royal Choral Society and Royal Albert Hall Orchestra at the Albert Hall on 2 April 1926. Handel’s short cries of praise grow into long notes that hang above the racing choral lines.

sections.label: A · Hallelujah in D major
sections.mNote: Strings introduce the rhythm; four choral parts answer

sections.label: B · The kingdom of this world
sections.mNote: The choir sings in measured crotchets

sections.label: C · King of kings
sections.mNote: Sopranos and altos hold A above the answers

sections.label: D · Long notes in the tenors
sections.mNote: The tenors sustain D beneath the quicker upper parts

sections.label: Coda · The last Hallelujah
sections.mNote: The bass moves from G to D

cues.title: Three bars before the choir
cues.text: The strings introduce the rhythm of “Hallelujah” before anyone sings. When the choir enters, all four parts speak together; the violins slip little answering phrases between the cries.
cues.evidence: Handel, Messiah, Hallelujah, bars 1–11; Joshua Koo’s Mutopia full score, violin and choral parts. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A sentence in crotchets
cues.text: “The kingdom of this world” slows the choir’s syllables to measured crotchets. The four parts move together, and the bass descends beneath them. After so many short cries, Handel lets a whole sentence unfold.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 33–41, the setting of “The kingdom of this world”. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: A tune passed upwards
cues.text: The basses start “And he shall reign”; tenors, altos and sopranos follow in turn. The tune leaps through the chord, then runs down in smaller steps.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 41–51; entries in bass, tenor, alto and soprano. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Inside the Albert Hall
cues.text: This is a concert at the Royal Albert Hall, preserved on disc on 2 April 1926. The Royal Choral Society sings with the hall’s orchestra; Malcolm Sargent conducts.
cues.evidence: German National Library catalogue, Electrola EJ 39, identifies a recording made during the 2 April 1926 concert: https://d-nb.info/380148439. Sargent’s credit: https://pool.publicdomainproject.org/index.php?title=Electrola-ej39-04871

cues.title: The sopranos keep climbing
cues.text: The sopranos take “King of kings” up to D, then climb through E and F♯ to G. Each note lasts across barlines. The lower voices keep answering, briskly, beneath that steadily rising line.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 57–68: sustained soprano proclamations on D, E, F♯ and G. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The word after the rest
cues.text: The quick repetitions stop, leaving a rest before the last “Hallelujah”. This time the word fills long notes. G in the bass settles on D, and the choir holds the final chord under a fermata.
cues.evidence: Mutopia full score, bars 92–94: rest, final declaration, plagal cadence and fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=459
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: He filled London theatres with Italian opera, then put an English-speaking chorus at the centre of the drama.
facts: Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; Hamburg’s opera orchestra; Italy, 1706–10
London from 1712; 25 Brook Street from 1723 until his death
British citizen from 1727; composer for the court, theatres and Foundling Hospital
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Handel was eighteen when he left Halle for Hamburg in 1703 and took a place in the opera orchestra. His father had been a barber-surgeon; his teacher Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow had taught him the organ, counterpoint and the habit of copying other people’s scores. He had enrolled at Halle’s university and worked as a church organist. Hamburg offered something noisier: a public theatre, singers to accompany and an audience that had bought tickets. His first opera, Almira, opened there in 1705, with German words and Italian arias.

In Italy he found patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Roman cardinals commissioned music from the young Protestant; Prince Ruspoli gave him singers and instrumentalists to write for. The Dixit Dominus of 1707 sends five choral parts racing through a Latin psalm, then makes them hold dissonant notes while the other voices move underneath. His chamber cantatas tried the same arts of persuasion with a single singer. Corelli’s Rome taught him what a violin could say beside a voice.
